Linear Classifiers and Margin-Based Models

In Tutorial 2 we classified data using a distance-based model (k-NN) and tree-based models (Decision Tree, Random Forest). In this tutorial we look at two models that instead learn a decision boundary directly in the feature space: logistic regression and the support vector machine (SVM).

Both models draw a boundary between classes, but they choose where to draw it differently. Logistic regression places the boundary to maximise the likelihood of the observed labels; it models the probability of each class. The SVM is a margin-based model: it places the boundary to maximise the margin, the gap between the boundary and the nearest data points of each class. Those nearest points are called the support vectors, and they alone define the boundary. Maximising this margin tends to improve generalisation and reduce overfitting. With the kernel trick, an SVM can also bend the boundary to separate classes that a straight line cannot.

We will train logistic regression to classify two-phase flow regimes, and an SVM to detect a pump failure in an evaporator.

Before anything else, import the libraries we will need. Copy the following into the top of your script:


import_libraries.py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay

Part A: Logistic Regression on Flow Regime

When a gas and a liquid flow together through a pipe (common in reboilers, condensers, pipelines and multiphase reactors), they arrange themselves into distinct flow regimes depending on their relative flow rates. Three regimes appear in this dataset:

Flow Regime Description
Stratified The liquid flows along the bottom of the pipe with gas above it (low velocities).
Slug Large gas pockets and liquid “slugs” travel along the pipe in an irregular, intermittent fashion.
Annular A fast gas core flows in the centre with a thin liquid film on the pipe wall (high gas velocity).

Knowing the flow regime matters because it governs pressure drop, heat transfer, and the risk of vibration or flooding. Here we will predict the regime from just two measurements: the superficial gas velocity and the superficial liquid velocity. Download the dataset to get started:


flow_regime.csv
﻿Gas_velocity_(m/s),Liq_velocity_(m/s),Flow
0.7,0.5,Slug
0.8,0.5,Slug
1,0.5,Slug
1.44,0.5,Slug
... (130 more lines)

Below is a description of each column in the dataset:

Feature Description
Gas_velocity_(m/s) Superficial gas velocity
Liq_velocity_(m/s) Superficial liquid velocity
Flow Flow regime: Annular, Slug, or Stratified (the label)
NoteHow does logistic regression work?

Logistic regression is a classification algorithm. It forms a linear combination of the features, \(z = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + b\), and passes it through the sigmoid (logistic) function \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\), which squashes the result into a probability between 0 and 1. The class is decided by whether this probability crosses 0.5. The set of points where it equals 0.5 is a straight line (a linear decision boundary) in feature space. For more than two classes, as we have here, scikit-learn fits a multinomial version that returns a probability for every class and predicts the most likely one (through the use of the softmax function).

Task 1 : Load the dataset

Write a function load_flow_regime_data that loads the dataset and returns the features X (a 2D array of the two velocities) and the labels y (a 1D array). Because the labels are text ("Annular", "Slug", "Stratified"), use scikit-learn’s LabelEncoder to convert them to integers (0, 1, 2). The function should also return the class names so we can label plots later, and print the shapes to confirm the data loaded correctly.

TipEncoding text labels with LabelEncoder

LabelEncoder turns a column of text categories into integers. First define an encoder object via LabelEncoder(), and then use it to apply it to the relevant data: encoder.fit_transform(column). You can then use encoder.classes_ afterwards to recover the original names in integer order (0, 1, 2, …). See the attached documentation for more: scikit-learn.

load_flow_regime_data.py
def load_flow_regime_data(file_path):
    """
    Load the flow regime dataset and return the features, labels, and class names.

    Parameters
    ----------
    file_path : str
        The path to the CSV file containing the dataset.

    Returns
    -------
    X : np.ndarray
        A 2D array of shape (n_samples, 2) containing the velocity features.
    y : np.ndarray
        A 1D array of integer-encoded flow regime labels.
    class_names : np.ndarray
        The original text label for each integer class.
    """
    # Load the dataset (utf-8-sig strips the byte-order mark on the first column)
    data = pd.read_csv(file_path, encoding="utf-8-sig")

    # Features: the two velocity columns. Labels: the flow regime, encoded to integers.
    X = data.iloc[:, :2].values
    encoder = LabelEncoder()
    y = encoder.fit_transform(data["Flow"])
    class_names = encoder.classes_

    print(f"Features shape: {X.shape}")
    print(f"Labels shape: {y.shape}")
    print(f"Classes: {list(class_names)}")
    return X, y, class_names

X, y, class_names = load_flow_regime_data('data/flow_regime.csv')

Task 2 : Visualise the data in log-space

Both velocities span more than an order of magnitude, so we first apply a log₁₀ transform. This spreads the data out evenly and, as you will see, makes the three regimes separate along roughly straight lines, exactly the kind of boundary logistic regression can draw. Create the transformed feature array:

X_log = np.log10(X)

Now write a function plot_flow_regime that produces a scatter plot of the (log-transformed) gas velocity against the liquid velocity, colouring each point by its flow regime. Your plot should look like the figure below.

>>>
plot_flow_regime(X_log, y, class_names)

NoteWhy the log-transform?

Superficial velocities in multiphase flow commonly range over several orders of magnitude, so on linear axes the low-velocity points bunch together in one corner. Taking the logarithm stretches them apart and, physically, flow-regime maps are conventionally drawn on log–log axes for exactly this reason (recall the moody diagram!).

Callout-answerAnswer 

plot_flow_regime.py
def plot_flow_regime(X, y, class_names):
    """
    Scatter plot of the two (log-transformed) velocity features, coloured by flow regime.

    Parameters
    ----------
    X : np.ndarray
        A 2D array of features (log-transformed velocities).
    y : np.ndarray
        A 1D array of integer-encoded labels.
    class_names : np.ndarray
        The text label for each integer class.
    """
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    for i, name in enumerate(class_names):
        plt.scatter(X[y == i, 0], X[y == i, 1], color=f"C{i}", label=name, edgecolor="k")
    plt.xlabel("log$_{10}$(Gas velocity)")
    plt.ylabel("log$_{10}$(Liquid velocity)")
    plt.title("Flow Regime Map")
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    plt.show()

plot_flow_regime(X_log, y, class_names)

Task 3 : Split into training and testing sets

As in Tutorial 2, we split the data so that we can estimate performance on unseen samples. Write a function preprocess_data that splits the features and labels into training and testing sets using train_test_split, with a test_size of 0.2 and a random_state of 42 for reproducibility.

>>>
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = preprocess_data(X_log, y)

Note

Notice we split the log-transformed features (X_log), not the raw velocities. Any transformation of the features happens before the split; the split only decides which rows are used for training and which are held back for testing.

Callout-answerAnswer 

preprocess_data.py
def preprocess_data(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42):
    """
    Split the features and labels into training and testing sets.

    Parameters
    ----------
    X : np.ndarray
        The feature array.
    y : np.ndarray
        The label array.
    test_size : float, optional
        The proportion of the data to hold back for testing (default is 0.2).
    random_state : int, optional
        The random seed for reproducibility (default is 42).

    Returns
    -------
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test : np.ndarray
        The training and testing features and labels.
    """
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
        X, y, test_size=test_size, random_state=random_state)
    return X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = preprocess_data(X_log, y)
print(X_train.shape, X_test.shape, y_train.shape, y_test.shape)
Output
(106, 2) (27, 2) (106,) (27,)
TipDo we need to scale the features here?

For an SVM we will (Part B), but here the two features are already on a similar scale after the log-transform, so scaling makes little difference to logistic regression. We keep the features in log-velocity units so the decision boundary we plot shortly stays physically interpretable.

Write a function train_logistic_regression that trains a LogisticRegression model on the training data, evaluates its accuracy on the test set, and returns both the trained model and the accuracy.

>>>
model, accuracy = train_logistic_regression(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test)

Callout-answerAnswer 

train_logistic_regression.py
def train_logistic_regression(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test):
    """
    Train a logistic regression classifier and evaluate it on the test set.

    Parameters
    ----------
    X_train, y_train : np.ndarray
        The training features and labels.
    X_test, y_test : np.ndarray
        The testing features and labels.

    Returns
    -------
    model : LogisticRegression
        The trained logistic regression model.
    accuracy : float
        The accuracy of the model on the test set.
    """
    # Create and train the logistic regression model
    model = LogisticRegression()
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)

    # Evaluate accuracy on the held-out test set
    accuracy = model.score(X_test, y_test)
    return model, accuracy

model, accuracy = train_logistic_regression(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test)
print(f"Logistic regression test accuracy: {accuracy:.3f}")

Task 5 : Evaluate with a confusion matrix

A confusion matrix shows which classes the model confuses, and is much more useful than a raw accuracy score. Each row is a true class and each column is a predicted class, so correct predictions sit on the diagonal and mistakes appear off it. Write a function plot_confusion_matrix that displays the confusion matrix for a fitted model using scikit-learn’s ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_estimator.

TipDrawing the matrix with ConfusionMatrixDisplay

ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_estimator(model, X_test, y_test) runs the model on the test set and plots the matrix in a single call. See the attached documentation for more: scikit-learn.

>>>
plot_confusion_matrix(model, X_test, y_test, class_names)

NoteReading a confusion matrix

Here the matrix is entirely on the diagonal: the model classifies every test point correctly. That is possible because the three regimes are so cleanly separated in log-space. On a messier, real-world dataset you would expect to see some off-diagonal entries, and those are usually where the interesting engineering questions live.

Callout-answerAnswer 

plot_confusion_matrix.py
def plot_confusion_matrix(model, X_test, y_test, class_names):
    """
    Display the confusion matrix for a fitted classifier on the test set.

    Parameters
    ----------
    model : fitted scikit-learn classifier
        The trained model to evaluate.
    X_test, y_test : np.ndarray
        The testing features and labels.
    class_names : np.ndarray
        The text label for each class (used to label the axes).
    """
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
    ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_estimator(
        model, X_test, y_test,
        display_labels=class_names, cmap="Blues", ax=ax)
    ax.set_title("Confusion Matrix")
    plt.show()

plot_confusion_matrix(model, X_test, y_test, class_names)

Task 6 : Visualise the decision boundary

The clearest way to understand a two-feature classifier is to draw its decision boundary: the regions of feature space it assigns to each class. We do this by evaluating the model on a fine grid of points covering the plot, colouring each grid point by its predicted class, and then overlaying the real data. Write a function plot_decision_boundary that does this.

TipThe NumPy helpers for building and evaluating a grid

Drawing a decision boundary will require the following NumPy and Matplotlib helpers functions:

  • np.meshgrid(xs, ys): turns those two 1D axes into a 2D grid of coordinates, xx and yy, covering the whole plot.
  • .ravel(): flattens the 2D xx/yy into 1D so every grid point can be fed to the model.
  • np.c_[a, b]: stacks the two flattened arrays column-wise into the (n, 2) shape that model.predict expects.
  • .reshape(xx.shape): folds the 1D predictions back into the grid’s 2D shape so they can be plotted.
  • plt.contourf(xx, yy, Z): fills each grid region with the colour of its predicted class.
>>>
plot_decision_boundary(model, X_log, y, class_names)

Notice that the boundaries between regions are straight lines; this is the defining feature of logistic regression. Because the classes separate so well in log-space, those straight lines are enough to classify every point correctly.

Callout-answerAnswer 

plot_decision_boundary.py
def plot_decision_boundary(model, X, y, class_names):
    """
    Plot the decision regions of a fitted two-feature classifier, with the data overlaid.

    Parameters
    ----------
    model : fitted scikit-learn classifier
        The trained model whose boundary is drawn.
    X : np.ndarray
        A 2D feature array (the same features the model was trained on).
    y : np.ndarray
        The integer-encoded labels.
    class_names : np.ndarray
        The text label for each class.
    """
    # Build a grid of points spanning the feature space
    x_min, x_max = X[:, 0].min() - 0.5, X[:, 0].max() + 0.5
    y_min, y_max = X[:, 1].min() - 0.5, X[:, 1].max() + 0.5
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(x_min, x_max, 300),
                         np.linspace(y_min, y_max, 300))

    # Predict the class for every grid point
    Z = model.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).reshape(xx.shape)

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    plt.contourf(xx, yy, Z, alpha=0.2,
                 levels=np.arange(len(class_names) + 1) - 0.5,
                 colors=[f"C{i}" for i in range(len(class_names))])
    for i, name in enumerate(class_names):
        plt.scatter(X[y == i, 0], X[y == i, 1], color=f"C{i}", label=name, edgecolor="k")
    plt.xlabel("log$_{10}$(Gas velocity)")
    plt.ylabel("log$_{10}$(Liquid velocity)")
    plt.title("Logistic Regression Decision Boundary")
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

plot_decision_boundary(model, X_log, y, class_names)
Output

Task 7 : Explore the regularisation strength C

Logistic regression has a hyperparameter C that controls regularisation: how strongly the model is penalised for using large coefficients. A small C means strong regularisation (a simpler, flatter model that may underfit); a large C means weak regularisation (the model is free to fit the training data closely). Write a function explore_C that trains the model for a range of C values and plots the resulting test accuracy. Because C spans several orders of magnitude, use a logarithmic x-axis.

The example usage of the function is provided below, along with the output plot:

>>>
C_values = np.logspace(-3, 3, 20)
>>>
explore_C(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, C_values)

Looking at the plot, what happens to the accuracy when C is very small? Why?

Callout-answerAnswer 

explore_C.py
def explore_C(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, C_values):
    """
    Evaluate logistic regression accuracy across a range of regularisation strengths.

    Parameters
    ----------
    X_train, y_train : np.ndarray
        The training features and labels.
    X_test, y_test : np.ndarray
        The testing features and labels.
    C_values : array-like
        The values of C to evaluate.
    """
    accuracies = []
    for C in C_values:
        model = LogisticRegression(C=C)
        model.fit(X_train, y_train)
        accuracies.append(model.score(X_test, y_test))

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
    ax.plot(C_values, accuracies, marker='o')
    ax.set_xscale('log')
    ax.set_title('Accuracy of Logistic Regression for Different Values of C')
    ax.set_xlabel('Regularisation strength C (log scale)')
    ax.set_ylabel('Accuracy')
    ax.grid(True)
    plt.show()

C_values = np.logspace(-3, 3, 20)
explore_C(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, C_values)
Output

At very small C the regularisation is so strong that the model’s coefficients are shrunk almost to zero. The model can barely distinguish the classes and underfits badly, so accuracy collapses. As C increases, the penalty relaxes, the boundary sharpens, and accuracy climbs to 100% and plateaus. Because this dataset is cleanly separable, there is no overfitting penalty at large C, but on noisier data, an excessively large C can overfit the training set and reduce test accuracy.

Part B: Support Vector Machines for Fault Detection

An evaporator concentrates a solution by boiling off solvent. This dataset comes from a simulated forced-circulation evaporator (the classic Newell–Lee model) and records three process measurements together with the plant’s operating status. Half of the records are from normal operation, and half are from operation during a pump failure. Our task is a fault-detection problem: can we tell, from the process measurements alone, whether the pump has failed? Download the dataset:


evap_data.csv
﻿L2,P2,X2,Status
1.044822916,50.39874027,27.08635423,Normal
1.008144051,50.27810345,22.92532847,Normal
1.020358578,51.45807588,26.58529487,Normal
0.97448334,50.50077586,24.56927528,Normal
... (998 more lines)

Below is a description of each column in the dataset:

Feature Description
L2 Separator liquid level
P2 Operating pressure
X2 Product composition (concentration)
Status Operating status: Normal or Pump_failure (the label)
NoteHow does a support vector machine work?

An SVM looks for the decision boundary (a hyperplane) that separates the classes with the widest possible margin: the largest gap on either side before hitting a data point. The points sitting on the edge of that margin are the support vectors, and they alone define the boundary; moving any other point does not change it. A soft margin, controlled by the hyperparameter C, allows a few points to fall inside the margin or on the wrong side, trading a little training accuracy for a simpler, more general boundary.

When the classes cannot be separated by a straight line, the kernel trick implicitly maps the data into a higher-dimensional space where a linear boundary does exist. The rbf (radial basis function) and poly (polynomial) kernels do exactly this, producing curved boundaries in the original feature space, whereas the linear kernel keeps the boundary straight.

def load_evap_data(file_path):
    """
    Load the evaporator dataset and return the features, labels, and class names.

    Parameters
    ----------
    file_path : str
        The path to the CSV file containing the dataset.

    Returns
    -------
    X : np.ndarray
        A 2D array of shape (n_samples, 3) containing the process measurements.
    y : np.ndarray
        A 1D array of integer-encoded status labels (0 = Normal, 1 = Pump_failure).
    class_names : np.ndarray
        The original text label for each integer class.
    """
    # Load the dataset (utf-8-sig strips the byte-order mark on the first column)
    data = pd.read_csv(file_path, encoding="utf-8-sig")

    # Features: the three process measurements. Labels: the status, encoded to integers.
    X = data.iloc[:, :3].values
    encoder = LabelEncoder()
    y = encoder.fit_transform(data["Status"])
    class_names = encoder.classes_

    print(f"Features shape: {X.shape}")
    print(f"Labels shape: {y.shape}")
    print(f"Classes: {list(class_names)}")
    return X, y, class_names

def explore_evap_data(X, y, class_names):
    """
    Print summary statistics and the class distribution, and scatter P2 against X2.

    Parameters
    ----------
    X : np.ndarray
        The feature array (columns L2, P2, X2).
    y : np.ndarray
        The integer-encoded labels.
    class_names : np.ndarray
        The text label for each class.
    """
    feature_names = ["L2", "P2", "X2"]
    df = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=feature_names)

    print("Summary statistics of features:")
    print(df.describe().round(2))
    print("Label distribution:")
    for i, name in enumerate(class_names):
        print(f"  {name}: {(y == i).sum()}")

    # Scatter plot of P2 vs X2, coloured by status
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    for i, name in enumerate(class_names):
        plt.scatter(X[y == i, 1], X[y == i, 2], color=f"C{i}", label=name, alpha=0.5, s=15)
    plt.xlabel("P2 (operating pressure)")
    plt.ylabel("X2 (product composition)")
    plt.title("Evaporator Data: P2 vs X2 by Status")
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Task 10 : Preprocess (split and scale)

This time we must scale the features. Write a function preprocess_and_scale that first splits the data (test size 0.2, random state 42), then standardises the features with StandardScaler. Crucially, the scaler is fitted on the training set only and then used to transform both sets, so no information about the test data leaks into training. Return the scaled splits.

Tipfit_transform vs transform

StandardScaler gives you two methods you must not mix up. Call scaler.fit_transform(X_train) on the training data: this learns each feature’s mean and standard deviation and applies them in one step. Then call scaler.transform(X_test) on the test data: this reuses the values already learned from the training set. Never call fit (or fit_transform) on the test set, or test information leaks into your scaling. See the StandardScaler docs.

>>>
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = preprocess_and_scale(X, y)
>>>
X_train.shape, X_test.shape, y_train.shape, y_test.shape
 
((800, 3), (201, 3), (800,), (201,))
ImportantWhy scale the features for an SVM?

An SVM cares about distances between points: directly for the rbf kernel, and through the margin for every kernel. If one feature ranged over 0–1000 and another over 0–1, the first would dominate every distance and the model would effectively ignore the second. Standardising each feature to zero mean and unit variance puts them on an equal footing. (This is why scaling mattered far less for logistic regression in Part A, where both log-velocity features were already comparable.)

Callout-answerAnswer 

preprocess_and_scale.py
def preprocess_and_scale(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42):
    """
    Split the data, then standardise the features (fitting the scaler on the training set only).

    Parameters
    ----------
    X : np.ndarray
        The feature array.
    y : np.ndarray
        The label array.
    test_size : float, optional
        The proportion of the data to hold back for testing (default is 0.2).
    random_state : int, optional
        The random seed for reproducibility (default is 42).

    Returns
    -------
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test : np.ndarray
        The scaled training and testing features, and their labels.
    """
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
        X, y, test_size=test_size, random_state=random_state)

    scaler = StandardScaler()
    X_train = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)   # fit on training data only
    X_test = scaler.transform(X_test)         # apply the same scaling to the test data
    return X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = preprocess_and_scale(X, y)
print(X_train.shape, X_test.shape, y_train.shape, y_test.shape)

Task 11 : Train a support vector machine

Write a function train_svm that trains a support vector classifier (SVC) on the training data, evaluates its accuracy on the test set, and returns both the model and the accuracy. Expose the kernel, C, and gamma settings as arguments so we can experiment with them, and start with a linear kernel.

>>>
svm_model, accuracy = train_svm(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, kernel="linear")
>>>
print(f"Linear SVM test accuracy: {accuracy:.3f}")
 
Linear SVM test accuracy: 0.995
Callout-answerAnswer 

train_svm.py
def train_svm(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, kernel="linear", C=1.0, gamma="scale"):
    """
    Train a support vector classifier and evaluate it on the test set.

    Parameters
    ----------
    X_train, y_train : np.ndarray
        The training features and labels.
    X_test, y_test : np.ndarray
        The testing features and labels.
    kernel : str, optional
        The SVM kernel: "linear", "rbf", or "poly" (default is "linear").
    C : float, optional
        The soft-margin regularisation strength (default is 1.0).
    gamma : str or float, optional
        The kernel coefficient for "rbf"/"poly" (default is "scale").

    Returns
    -------
    model : SVC
        The trained support vector classifier.
    accuracy : float
        The accuracy of the model on the test set.
    """
    model = SVC(kernel=kernel, C=C, gamma=gamma)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    accuracy = model.score(X_test, y_test)
    return model, accuracy

svm_model, accuracy = train_svm(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, kernel="linear")
print(f"Linear SVM test accuracy: {accuracy:.3f}")

Task 12 : Compare kernels

The real flexibility of an SVM comes from its kernel. Write a function compare_kernels that trains an SVM with each kernel in a supplied list, prints the test accuracy of each, and draws a bar chart comparing them.

>>>
kernels = ["linear", "rbf", "poly"]
>>>
compare_kernels(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, kernels)
 
linear kernel: accuracy = 0.995
 
rbf kernel: accuracy = 0.995
 
poly kernel: accuracy = 0.995

All three kernels achieve very similar accuracy here. What does that tell you about how separable the two classes are, and which kernel would you choose?

Callout-answerAnswer 

compare_kernels.py
def compare_kernels(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, kernels):
    """
    Train an SVM with each kernel and compare their test accuracy.

    Parameters
    ----------
    X_train, y_train : np.ndarray
        The training features and labels.
    X_test, y_test : np.ndarray
        The testing features and labels.
    kernels : list of str
        The kernels to compare, e.g. ["linear", "rbf", "poly"].
    """
    accuracies = []
    for kernel in kernels:
        model, accuracy = train_svm(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, kernel=kernel)
        accuracies.append(accuracy)
        print(f"{kernel:>8} kernel: accuracy = {accuracy:.3f}")

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
    ax.bar(kernels, accuracies, alpha=0.7)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_title("SVM Accuracy by Kernel")
    ax.set_xlabel("Kernel")
    ax.set_ylabel("Accuracy")
    for i, acc in enumerate(accuracies):
        ax.text(i, acc + 0.02, f"{acc:.3f}", ha="center")
    plt.show()

kernels = ["linear", "rbf", "poly"]
compare_kernels(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, kernels)
Output
  linear kernel: accuracy = 0.995
     rbf kernel: accuracy = 0.995
    poly kernel: accuracy = 0.995
Output

The kernels perform almost identically because the two classes are very nearly linearly separable: a straight boundary already gets almost everything right, so the extra flexibility of the rbf and poly kernels buys nothing. When several models tie, prefer the simplest one: the linear kernel is fastest and least prone to overfitting. A curved kernel like rbf only pays off when the true boundary between the classes is itself curved.

Task 13 : Evaluate with a confusion matrix

For a fault-detection problem the type of error matters: a missed pump failure (a false negative) is very different from a false alarm (a false positive). Reuse the plot_confusion_matrix function you wrote in Part A (it works with any fitted scikit-learn classifier) to inspect the errors made by the linear SVM.

>>>
plot_confusion_matrix(svm_model, X_test, y_test, class_names)

NoteFalse positives vs false negatives

In a binary fault-detection setting the off-diagonal entries have names:

  • A false negative (a real Pump_failure predicted as Normal) means a genuine fault went undetected, usually the more dangerous error.
  • A false positive (a Normal case flagged as Pump_failure) is a false alarm: annoying and costly, but safer.

Which of these would you be more willing to tolerate on a real plant? The answer shapes how you would tune the model.

Task 14 : Visualise the decision boundary and support vectors

Finally, let us see the SVM at work. Our model uses all three features, which we cannot draw, so to visualise the boundary we train a separate SVM on just two features, P2 and X2, and plot its decision regions, overlaying the training data and circling the support vectors. Write a function plot_svm_decision_boundary that does this, using an rbf kernel so we can see a curved boundary.

TipFinding the support vectors

Once an SVC is fitted, its support vectors are stored on the model as the attribute model.support_vectors_; an array of their coordinates. Scatter these on top of the plot (for example as open circles, using facecolors="none") to highlight the handful of points that actually define the boundary. The grid-plotting helpers (np.meshgrid, .ravel(), np.c_, plt.contourf) are the same ones introduced in the Part A decision-boundary task. See the documentation for more: scikit-learn.

>>>
plot_svm_decision_boundary(X_train, y_train, class_names)

The black circles are the support vectors; the points closest to the boundary, which are the only ones that determine where it sits. Notice how they line the border between the two clusters, while points deep inside each cluster are ignored entirely. Unlike the straight lines of logistic regression, the rbf kernel lets this boundary curve to follow the shape of the data.

Callout-answerAnswer 

plot_svm_decision_boundary.py
def plot_svm_decision_boundary(X_train, y_train, class_names,
                               feature_idx=(1, 2), feature_names=("P2", "X2"), kernel="rbf"):
    """
    Train a two-feature SVM and plot its decision regions with the support vectors circled.

    Parameters
    ----------
    X_train : np.ndarray
        The (scaled) training features.
    y_train : np.ndarray
        The training labels.
    class_names : np.ndarray
        The text label for each class.
    feature_idx : tuple of int, optional
        Which two feature columns to use (default (1, 2) = P2 and X2).
    feature_names : tuple of str, optional
        Display names for the two chosen features.
    kernel : str, optional
        The SVM kernel to use for the plot (default "rbf").
    """
    # Train a fresh SVM on just the two chosen features
    X2d = X_train[:, feature_idx]
    model = SVC(kernel=kernel).fit(X2d, y_train)

    # Build a grid and predict the class at every grid point
    x_min, x_max = X2d[:, 0].min() - 0.5, X2d[:, 0].max() + 0.5
    y_min, y_max = X2d[:, 1].min() - 0.5, X2d[:, 1].max() + 0.5
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(x_min, x_max, 300),
                         np.linspace(y_min, y_max, 300))
    Z = model.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).reshape(xx.shape)

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    plt.contourf(xx, yy, Z, alpha=0.2, levels=[-0.5, 0.5, 1.5], colors=["C0", "C1"])
    for i, name in enumerate(class_names):
        plt.scatter(X2d[y_train == i, 0], X2d[y_train == i, 1],
                    color=f"C{i}", label=name, alpha=0.5, s=15)
    # Circle the support vectors
    plt.scatter(model.support_vectors_[:, 0], model.support_vectors_[:, 1],
                s=60, facecolors="none", edgecolors="k", label="Support vectors")
    plt.xlabel(f"{feature_names[0]} (standardised)")
    plt.ylabel(f"{feature_names[1]} (standardised)")
    plt.title(f"SVM Decision Boundary ({kernel} kernel)")
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

plot_svm_decision_boundary(X_train, y_train, class_names)
Output

Conclusion

By the end of this tutorial, you should understand two of the most widely used linear classifiers. Logistic regression draws a straight-line boundary by modelling class probabilities, and its C hyperparameter controls regularisation. The support vector machine draws the maximum-margin boundary, defined by a handful of support vectors, and its kernel lets it bend that boundary to fit non-linear data. Along the way you also met two evaluation tools that go beyond a single accuracy number (the confusion matrix and the decision boundary plot) and saw why feature scaling matters for distance-based models like the SVM.

A recurring theme is worth restating: when several models perform equally well, prefer the simplest. Both datasets here turned out to be close to linearly separable, so the simplest boundary was already the best one.
